blocks.text: Daniel's text survives in multiple manuscripts from Qumran, preserved in both Hebrew and Aramaic, attesting to its circulation and authority in late Second Temple Judaism. Similarly, Jeremiah—the text Daniel reads and reinterprets—is known from five Qumran manuscripts (conventionally designated 4QJer-a through 4QJer-e), which contain readings that differ at points from later Masoretic and Greek forms. These witnesses document how both texts were transmitted and engaged during this period. Other Qumran literature preserves related but distinct Danielic traditions, such as the Prayer of Nabonidus, suggesting a broader Danielic literary corpus.

Daniel's prayer in chapter 9 established a model of Danielic intercession that later traditions expanded significantly. Greek manuscripts of Daniel preserve additional material—the Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three, the narrative of Susanna, and Bel and the Dragon—that enlarge the Danielic corpus. These additions emphasize extended prayer and praise, wisdom and justice, and strong anti-idolatry polemic. They attest to the flexibility of Danielic tradition in Jewish religious practice, where the figure and writings of Daniel served as a vehicle for liturgical reflection on divine justice and vindication.
